summary: A mid-sized software company in Leeds implemented a four-day work week with no pay cut, resulting in an 8% decrease in project delivery times and a significant reduction in staff turnover. Similar trials across Europe and North America have shown promising results, with most companies choosing to keep the policy after the trial ended.
important_points: A mid-sized software company in Leeds implemented a four-day work week with no pay cut and saw an 8% decrease in project delivery times and a significant reduction in staff turnover.
Similar trials across Europe and North America have shown promising results, with most companies choosing to keep the policy after the trial ended.
The four-day work week model is based on the '100-80-100' principle: 100% pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% output.
Supporters argue that the gains come from focus rather than hours, with teams cutting low-value meetings and automating repetitive tasks.
Customer-facing businesses struggle to reduce hours without hiring more staff, but rotating schedules can help maintain coverage.
target_audience: Business owners and managers considering implementing a four-day work week in their organizations, as well as HR professionals and labor experts interested in the topic.
